newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Greek Cypriots make goodwill visit to N.Cyprus.
newsitem.headline: Greek Cypriots make goodwill visit to N.Cyprus.

text.p: More than 600 Greek Cypriots made a rare pilgrimage to a monastery in the Turkish-held part of Cyprus on Friday, the first since Turkey invaded the eastern Mediterranean island in 1974.

A bus convoy carrying 652 Greek Cypriots with United Nations escorts set off from the U.N.-controlled Ledra Palace checkpoint, the only authorised crossing point between the north and south of the divided island. They returned on Friday evening.
They travelled to Apostolos Andreas, a monastery 125 km (80 miles) away on the tip of the northeastern Karpasia peninsula.

Youngsters, who had never been to the north of the ceasefire line slicing through Cyprus, and pensioners travelled more than 100 km (60 miles) overnight to be at the checkpoint as dawn broke over Cyprus's capital Nicosia.
The pilgrimage was one of a set of goodwill humanitarian gestures between the two sides to improve relations between Cyprus's estranged Greeks and Turks.
Instead of packing food and drinks, many took with them two metre-long candles, olive oil and icons.
Turkey invaded the north of Cyprus in 1974 in response to a brief Greek Cypriot coup engineered by the military ruling Greece. Since then very few Greek Cypriots have been able to visit the north.
A breakaway Turkish Cypriot state created there in 1983 is recognised only by Turkey.

The 652 Greek Cypriots from the south were joined by 219 Greek Cypriots from nearby villages in the north of the island who congregated at the church, situated at the picturesque tip of the island with panoramic views of surrounding countryside. The Greek Cypriots living in the north threw rose petals in the streets as the bus convoy passed through villages.

"It was a religious visit for me. Nothing political. I had the opportunity to meet my friends and relatives from the village where I was born, so I am happy," Nicos Fallas of the Karpasia Coordination Committee told Reuters. "But I am not very happy that Cyprus is not free," he said.
Fallas was banned from entering northern Cyprus during a previous crossing from the south.
The ceremony passed peacefully amid low-key security.
The monastery, built in 1867, is said to have been built on the spot where the Apostole Andrew, one of Jesus's first disciples, ran aground during a missionary journey.
Before 1974 Greek Cypriots would hold an annual three-day vigil there on August 15, the day of the Assumption of the Virgin. It is one of the most important holidays in the Greek Orthodox calendar.
